content: Garlic (Allium sativum), when used in combination with other agents, has specific dosing recommendations based on the condition being treated. It is applied to the affected area three times daily (TID) for various purposes, including prevention of cardiovascular disease, cancer prevention, circulation enhancement, treatment of Helicobacter pylori infections, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, immune stimulation, menstrual disorders, tick repellency, and tinea infections. While some data on its ability to reduce serum lipid levels are conflicting, overall, garlic has been shown to modestly decrease serum cholesterol levels. Garlic interacts with numerous medications and substances, often increasing anticoagulation effects. For example, when combined with drugs such as aceclofenac, aspirin, heparin, warfarin, or natural products like ginseng, ginger, or ginkgo biloba, garlic enhances the risk of bleeding. In such cases, caution is advised, and close monitoring is recommended. In some instances, therapy modification may be necessary. Garlic also decreases the levels of certain drugs, such as atazanavir, darunavir, and ritonavir, through unknown mechanisms, necessitating careful monitoring. Adverse effects associated with garlic include anaphylaxis, angioedema, asthma, bleeding, conjunctivitis, contact dermatitis (with topical use), diarrhea, eczema (with topical use), flatulence, gastrointestinal irritation or burning, gastrointestinal upset, heartburn, nausea, vomiting, rhinitis, and urticaria. Garlic use is contraindicated in individuals with bleeding disorders, those undergoing surgery within 1–2 weeks, and in cases of concurrent use with CYP3A4 substrates, diabetes mellitus, gastrointestinal infections, or inflammatory bowel disease. Regarding pregnancy and lactation, garlic is generally considered acceptable, with controlled studies in pregnant women showing no evidence of fetal risk. However, specific data on metabolism and excretion during pregnancy and lactation are not available. Garlic’s active constituent, allicin, inhibits cholesterol biosynthesis, platelet aggregation, thromboxane synthesis, and lysosomal enzyme release. It also reduces vascular muscle tone, contributing to its cardiovascular benefits. The cholesterol-lowering effects of garlic typically manifest within 8–16 weeks, while its hypotensive effects may take 1–6 months to become evident.
